planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in bright light in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; Flapjacks is grown outdoors year-round only in zone 9b-11, and needs container culture with winter protection further north.

directions: Grow in bright light, including several hours of direct sun, in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out. Flapjacks forms large, flat, paddle-shaped leaves stacked in an architectural rosette, powdery pale gray-green in shade and flushing a vivid coral-red along the leaf margins and eventually across the whole leaf surface with more direct sun and cooler temperatures, an eye-catching color display that makes it a popular accent plant in containers and succulent gardens. Mature plants send up a tall flower spike with small yellow blooms after several years, after which the rosette that flowered typically declines, though offsets usually continue the plant. Protect from frost, since it is not reliably hardy outside the warmest zones, and avoid overwatering, which quickly causes rot in the thick, water-storing leaves.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in bright light in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; Panda Plant is most often grown as a container and houseplant succulent, since it is not reliably hardy outdoors even in zone 9.

directions: Grow in bright light, including some direct sun, in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only when the soil has fully dried out. Panda Plant bears thick, fuzzy, silvery-gray leaves densely covered in fine white hairs, with distinctive rust-brown spots along the scalloped leaf edges that give the plant its common name and a soft, plush texture unusual among succulents. Its slow, upright growth and tactile appeal make it a popular houseplant and container succulent, best kept indoors on a bright windowsill or outdoors in full sun during warm months. Avoid getting the fuzzy leaves wet when watering, since trapped moisture on the hairy surface can encourage rot; water at the soil level instead. Bring indoors well before the first frost, since it has no meaningful cold tolerance.
